blocks.prompt: How a Tomato Grows
blocks.text: A tomato starts as a tiny yellow flower on a green plant. When the flower falls away, a small green tomato grows in its place. The tomato drinks up sunshine and water. Slowly it gets bigger. Slowly it turns from green to red. When it is red and soft, it is ripe and ready to pick. Inside every tomato are lots of little seeds. If you plant one seed, a whole new tomato plant can grow. People eat tomatoes in salad, on pizza, and in warm soup. Some tomatoes are as tiny as a marble. Some are as big as your hand.

blocks.prompt: The Fruit That Everyone Calls a Vegetable
blocks.text: Ask most people what a tomato is, and they will say it is a vegetable. Scientists say something different. A tomato grows from a flower and holds seeds inside, and that makes it a fruit. In fact, it is a kind of berry. Tomatoes did not always grow all over the world. Long ago they grew wild in South America, where the fruit was small and yellow. People in Mexico were the first to grow them for food. They called the fruit tomatl. When explorers carried tomato plants back to Europe, some people were afraid to eat them. They thought the bright red fruit might be poison. Today we know tomatoes are good to eat. A tomato turns red because of something inside it called lycopene. The riper the tomato, the redder it gets. Farmers grow thousands of kinds. Some are red, some are yellow, some are purple, and a few are striped like candy.

blocks.prompt: How a Fruit Won a Court Case as a Vegetable
blocks.text: The tomato lives a double life. To a botanist, the person who studies plants, the answer is simple. A tomato develops from the flower of the plant and carries the seeds, so it is a fruit, and more exactly a berry. To a cook, that answer is useless. Tomatoes are not sweet like apples or peaches. They belong in soups, sauces, and salads, next to onions and beans, so cooks have always treated them as vegetables. This argument once reached a court of law. In 1893, the United States taxed imported vegetables but not fruit. A trader named Nix wanted his tomatoes counted as fruit so he would not have to pay the tax. The Supreme Court disagreed. The judges decided that because people eat tomatoes with dinner and not for dessert, the law would treat them as vegetables. Science lost to the kitchen. The tomato has been surprising people for a long time. It began as a small wild plant in the Andes mountains of South America and was first farmed in Mexico. When Spanish ships carried it to Europe, many Europeans refused to eat it. The tomato belongs to the nightshade family, and some of its relatives really are poisonous. Wealthy families ate off pewter plates that contained lead, and the acid in tomatoes pulled the lead out, which made diners sick. For years people blamed the fruit instead of the plate. Only later did the tomato become one of the most eaten foods on Earth.

blocks.prompt: The Poison Apple That Fed the World
blocks.text: Few foods have traveled as far, or been misjudged as badly, as the tomato. Today it flavors pizza in Italy, curries in India, and salsa in Mexico, and it is easy to assume it has always belonged to those places. It has not. The tomato is a newcomer to almost every kitchen that now depends on it. The plant began in western South America, along the dry slopes of the Andes, where the wild fruit was no bigger than a pea. People in what is now Mexico were the first to tame it, growing larger fruit and giving it the name tomatl. When Spanish ships returned from the Americas in the 1500s, they carried tomato seeds back to Europe along with gold and new ideas. Europe was not grateful. The tomato belongs to the nightshade family, a group of plants that includes several genuine poisons, and its strange red fruit made people nervous. For roughly two hundred years, many Europeans grew the tomato only as a curious garden decoration and refused to put it on the table. There was even a grain of truth behind the fear. Rich households dined on plates made partly of lead, and the acid in tomatoes drew that lead into the food, slowly poisoning the very people who could afford such plates. The fruit took the blame for the plate's crime. What finally rescued the tomato was hunger and flavor. Poorer families, eating from wooden or clay dishes, had no lead to fear, and they discovered that the tomato made plain food delicious. In southern Italy it met wheat pasta and became a sauce the world would copy. By the 1800s the tomato had shed its dangerous reputation almost everywhere. Its comeback is remarkable. The tomato is now among the most grown fruits on the planet, and yes, it is a fruit, since it forms from a flower and holds its seeds inside. Thousands of varieties exist, from tiny sweet cherry types to beefsteaks as wide as a plate, in colors that run from deep red to yellow, orange, green, and near black. A plant once feared as poison now feeds more people than almost any other.

notes: Solanum lycopersicum, in the nightshade family
Botanically a berry, legally a vegetable in the US since 1893

Carried to Europe by Spanish ships in the 1500s

blocks.prompt: The Tomato: A Berry That Rewrote the World's Cooking
blocks.text: It is difficult to picture Italian cooking without tomato sauce, Indian curry without tomato gravy, or a Mexican table without salsa, and yet none of those cuisines knew the tomato until about five hundred years ago. The fruit that now seems native to half the world's kitchens is, historically speaking, a recent arrival everywhere except one corner of the Americas. Its journey from wild weed to global staple is a story of botany, fear, chemistry, and appetite. Botanically, the tomato is not a vegetable at all. It develops from the flower of the plant Solanum lycopersicum and encloses its seeds in fleshy pulp, which makes it a fruit and, more precisely, a berry. Cooks have never cared. Because the tomato is savory rather than sweet and shares a plate with onions and beans, kitchens have always filed it under vegetables. The disagreement became law in 1893, when the United States Supreme Court, deciding a tax case, ruled that tomatoes are vegetables because they are usually served at dinner and not, like fruits generally, as dessert. Science made its case and the kitchen won. The plant itself came from the western edge of South America, in the foothills of the Andes, where the wild fruit was tiny and sour. Farmers in what is now Mexico first domesticated it and called it tomatl, the root of the word we still use. Spanish ships carried its seeds to Europe in the sixteenth century, and there the tomato met a wall of suspicion. It belonged to the nightshade family, whose members include deadly plants, and its glossy red fruit looked more like a warning than a meal. For roughly two centuries many Europeans grew it only as an ornament. There was, oddly, real danger, though not from the fruit itself. The wealthy ate from pewter and lead-glazed plates, and the acid in tomatoes leached lead out of the metal and into the meal, causing sickness that people blamed on the tomato rather than the tableware. The poor, who ate from wood and earthenware, ran no such risk, and it was largely poorer cooks, especially in southern Italy, who proved how good the tomato could be. Paired with wheat pasta, it produced a sauce the rest of the world eventually imitated. By the nineteenth century the fear had faded and the tomato spread into cuisine after cuisine. Today it is one of the most widely grown fruits on Earth, bred into thousands of varieties: marble-sized cherry tomatoes, beefsteaks broad as a hand, and fruit colored red, yellow, orange, purple, green, and nearly black. The red ones owe their color to lycopene, a pigment that deepens as the fruit ripens. The tomato's history is a warning about trusting appearances. A fruit was mistaken for a vegetable, a harmless food was mistaken for a poison, and the real culprit, a lead plate, escaped blame entirely for years. What rescued the tomato was not an argument but a taste: once people cooked with it, its usefulness overwhelmed every rumor. The plant that Europe once grew as decoration and feared as death now feeds more people, in more countries, than almost any other fruit in the world.
